name: Facet
text: Build the Excava interface in Figma as a clickable prototype first. It lets us test flows and interactions without writing code, so we catch usability flaws early when changes cost nothing. The trade-off is we delay real data feeds, but that’s fine—we need to lock the user experience before optimizing for live data.

name: Pane
text: The real risk with a Figma prototype is that it can create unrealistic expectations, making users think the final product is more polished than it actually is. A better alternative might be to create a minimal, functional prototype with real data feeds, even if it's not as visually appealing, to test the actual user experience. This argument would be settled if we could see data on how often Figma prototypes lead to mismatched user expectations versus functional prototypes.

name: Facet
text:
We should build a live HTML/CSS prototype with real data feeds for the Excava interface, as this approach allows us to test the actual performance and usability of the interface with real data. This decision prioritizes functional accuracy over visual polish, which is a trade-off I'm willing to accept because it ensures we're building an interface that works as intended. By doing so, we can identify and fix technical issues early on, rather than risking surprises later on. The trade-off is that the initial prototype may not be as visually appealing as a Figma design, but this is a worthwhile sacrifice for the sake of functional reliability.

name: Pane
text: Pane: A live HTML/CSS prototype locks us into early technical debt—if the data fakes poorly, we’ll waste time unraveling assumptions later. A better alternative is to mock the API with a lightweight server (like the VeriTeknik proxy) so we test real flows without committing to backend decisions. Settle it by proving the mock can swap in real data in one day.

name: Lumen
text:
DECISION: Ship one live HTML/CSS demo of Excava’s core flow with mocked API data via VeriTeknik proxy *and* one Figma clickable prototype—both must validate usability and expectations without locking us into technical debt.

Result: A validated interface flow (real data feel) and a polished visual reference (user expectations), owned by Facet (HTML/CSS) and Pane (Figma).
